newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: More officials seek to flee North Korea - radio.
newsitem.headline: More officials seek to flee North Korea - radio.

text.p: A senior North Korean defector taking refuge in South Korea's embassy in Beijing has told a U.S. intelligence official that several other Pyongyang officials were also planning to flee, Seoul's state radio said on Monday.

Korea Broadcasting System and local newspapers said Hwang Jang-yop told an official from the U.S Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) that six to seven officials of North Korea's ruling Workers' Party wanted to seek political asylum.
The media reports did not give thier intended destinations.
South Korean officials said they were unaware of the move.
Hwang, a senior aide to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, has stayed in the South Korean mission in Beijing since Wednesday as China, an ally of Pyongyang, agonised over his fate.
North Korea has said South Korea kidnapped Hwang, a claim brushed aside by Seoul as "preposterous".
The media reports said Hwang had a 35-minute meeting with the U.S. official at the consular section of the South Korean office hours after he arrived there to seek asylum in South Korea.
Those who plan to flee the North include high-ranking Workers' Party officials, they added.
The leading Chosun Ilbo newspaper, quoting diplomatic sources in Beijing, reported Hwang told the U.S. official that he had made up his mind to seek asylum after consulting with "a number of people".
"Apart from me, there are other people who have decided to defect," Chosun Ilbo quoted Hwang as telling the U.S. official.
Hwang told the official that he did not mind going to the United States briefly before he could settle in South Korea, according to the newpaper.
Seoul's other newspapers carried similar reports on Monday.

In Beijing, security was tight around the South Korean mission, with armed Chinese police setting up a fortress-like defence wall, laying anti-tyre spikes across approaches and bringing in a huge water cannon truck.
Monday mark's Hwang's 74th birthday.

U.S. ambassador to the United Nations Bill Richardson said on Sunday Washington was closely watching developments involving North Korean defectors after two suspected North Korean gunmen shot and seriously wounded a prominent North Korean defector near Seoul on Saturday.
"This is an incident that is serious," Richardson said on ABC Television's "This Week" programme. "This is an incident that we're watching very closely."
Seoul officials said Li Il-nam, the nephew of North Korean leader Kim Jong-il's ex-wife, remained in coma on Monday in a hospital in Bundang, just south of Seoul.
They said they believed Li, known in South Korea as Lee Han-yong, was attacked by an assassionation squad sent by North Korea.
The assassination attempt appeared to be a warning to Seoul and to potential asylum-seekers, they added.
"If the South uses force to move him to South Korea we will respond with force," said one Pyongyang diplomat keeping watch outside the South Korean consular office in Beijing.
Richardson said U.S. intelligence analysts doubted North Korea was on the verge of collapse but were closely monitoring developments in the economically backward communist country.

"Our intelligence people claim that there is not a threat of an imminent collapse, but there's a tense situation there," Richardson said. "We have to watch it very closely. We're concerned about this defector situation.
